raw_response:
I’m 60 this year, and after farming this land for so many years, I still don’t like making big changes unless I see a clear reason. With only 7 mu and just two people in the house, I have to keep things steady and not spread cash too thin. Wheat and maize are still my backbone because they are reliable here, and the well gives me some confidence, but pumping water costs money, so I won’t water just for peace of mind. Cotton gives cash if the year is decent, and mungbean and red bean don’t need as much fertilizer, so I keep a little area in them to spread risk. I finished this plan mostly based on what has worked on my own fields, plus what other farmers around Quzhou are doing. The extension man says not to push too much nitrogen, but if the crop looks weak I usually still give a little extra rather than risk losing yield.

This year I’ll keep about 4.0 mu in the wheat-maize rotation, because that is the safest part of my farm income. The other 3.0 mu I’ll split between cotton, mungbean, and red bean. Cotton takes more labor, especially later, so I won’t plant too much of it at my age. For wheat I’ll use a normal base fertilizer and one topdress at jointing, then irrigate around the key stages if rainfall is short. Summer maize goes in right after wheat harvest, very fast, with light tillage or direct planting if I can get it done quickly. Mungbean and red bean are my low-input crops. I don’t expect the highest return from them every year, but they don’t tie up too much cash, and if weather turns bad they are not as painful as overinvesting in everything.

I left only a small area for cotton because it brings cash but needs more labor and management, and with just two people at home I cannot push too much. I also kept some mungbean and red bean because they need less fertilizer and give me a safer low-cost option.
